title: He Won the World Championship Seven Months Ago. At Norway Chess, Gukesh Is in Last Place.
excerpt: Three classical defeats, a 25-point rating slide, and a drop to world number 22. The youngest world champion in history is learning what the title costs.
body:
In December 2024, Dommaraju Gukesh became the youngest world chess champion in history at the age of 18, dethroning Ding Liren in a dramatic final game in Singapore. Seven months later, he is in last place at one of the strongest tournaments on the calendar.

Through eight rounds at Norway Chess 2026 in Oslo, Gukesh has accumulated just 8 points — trailing tournament leader Wesley So by 5.5 points and sitting behind every other competitor in the six-player field. He has lost three classical games: to Alireza Firouzja (twice, effectively) and to Praggnanandhaa in a battle of India's two brightest young stars.

The rating damage has been significant. Gukesh has lost 6.3 Elo points in Oslo alone, dropping to 22nd on the live world rankings — a position no reigning world champion has occupied in recent memory. Since the start of 2026, his cumulative rating loss exceeds 25 points, a slide that began at the Tata Steel Masters in January and continued through a difficult Prague event.

## The Time Management Problem

A pattern has emerged across Gukesh's losses. The deep calculation style that carried him to the world championship — the willingness to spend 15 or 20 minutes on a critical middlegame decision — has become a liability when the games extend beyond move 30.

Against Firouzja in Round 8, Gukesh sprung an opening novelty on move seven in the Ragozin Defence. It was part of his preparation. Then, on move 11, he froze for seven minutes and castled instead of playing the critical h4 push. He later admitted he had mixed up his preparation lines.

"I came up with this new ...Bf5, but I think he reacted in the best way possible, and I just forgot my prep," Gukesh told the Norway Chess confessional booth. "I'm pretty sure I mixed up something."

The resulting pawn-down endgame was holdable in theory, but with only 12 minutes on the clock, Gukesh could not find the defensive resources. Firouzja converted cleanly.

Against Praggnanandhaa in the earlier rounds, a similar dynamic played out — Gukesh reaching objectively reasonable positions but running low on time at the critical juncture.

## The Weight of the Crown

Gukesh has been candid about the adjustment. Being world champion means every game carries additional psychological pressure, every tournament becomes a referendum on whether the title was deserved. The expectations are not abstract: they come from a nation of 1.4 billion people and a chess community that has celebrated his rise as a generational achievement.

At the same time, the tournament format at Norway Chess — featuring Armageddon tiebreakers after every drawn classical game — punishes the kind of conservative approach a struggling player might use to stop the bleeding. Gukesh has had to fight for every half-point, and the relentless pace of six players facing each other in a round-robin has given him no easy pairings.

## The Company He Keeps in Struggle

Gukesh is not the only elite player having a difficult Oslo. Magnus Carlsen, the world number one, has lost four classical games — his worst such tally in a single event since Norway Chess 2015. Carlsen sits at 9 points, only one ahead of Gukesh, and has been beaten twice in classical play by Praggnanandhaa.

The Indian contingent's fortunes have been mixed overall. Praggnanandhaa, after a rocky start that included back-to-back losses in Rounds 5 and 6, has surged with consecutive classical victories over Firouzja and Carlsen to reach 9 points. In the women's section, Divya Deshmukh sits in second place with 10 points, while Koneru Humpy is in last with 6.5 points.

## What Comes Next

Two rounds remain. Gukesh faces Praggnanandhaa in Round 9 on Thursday — an all-Indian battle that could shape the final standings. In the last round on Friday, he will play Carlsen.

"I'm feeling pretty optimistic," Gukesh said after his Round 8 loss, a statement that felt less like bravado and more like the practiced resilience of a teenager who has been through worse. He won the Candidates at 17. He won the World Championship at 18. A bad tournament at 19 is a data point, not a verdict.

But the rating list is less forgiving than the history books. World number 22 is a long way from where a reigning world champion expects to be. The road back starts Thursday in Oslo.
